--- page 1 ---
Attention and Working Memory: A Review
Department of Psychology, Course Reader
Working memory is the small mental workspace we use to hold and change information for a few seconds.
It lets us follow a conversation, do sums in our heads and keep track of a plan while we carry it out.
Early models treated it as a single store with a fixed number of slots.
Later work showed that it is better described as a set of parts that cooperate.
A phonological loop holds sounds and words, a visuospatial sketchpad holds images, and a central executive directs attention between them.
Attention and working memory are closely linked.
When we attend to something, it is far more likely to enter working memory.
When working memory is full, our ability to attend to new events drops sharply.
LEFT-END RIGHT-START This link helps to explain everyday slips, such as walking into a room and forgetting why we came.
It also explains why people who are tired or anxious find it harder to concentrate.
Researchers measure working memory with span tasks.
In a simple span task, a person hears a list of digits and repeats them in order.
In a complex span task, the person must also solve a small problem between items.
Scores on complex span tasks predict reading comprehension, reasoning and exam results.
Training studies have tried to raise these scores through daily practice.
Most find that people improve on the trained task but not on other tasks.
--- page 2 ---
The idea of a limited capacity has a long history.
In 1956, George Miller suggested that people can hold about seven items at once.
Later researchers argued that the true limit is closer to four once rehearsal and chunking are taken into account.
Chunking groups separate items into larger meaningful units.
A string of twelve letters is hard to remember, but the same letters grouped into four familiar acronyms are easy.
Experts rely heavily on chunking.
A chess master can glance at a board from a real game and rebuild it almost perfectly.
When the pieces are placed at random, the master does no better than a beginner.
This shows that expertise works by building larger chunks, not by enlarging the store itself.
Forgetting in working memory has two main explanations.
Decay theory says that traces fade with time unless they are refreshed.
Interference theory says that new information pushes out or blurs the old.
Experiments that control both time and the number of intervening items tend to favour interference.
Even so, many researchers think both processes play a part.
The practical lesson is that rehearsal helps, and that switching between similar tasks makes forgetting worse.
Spacing similar topics apart in a study plan reduces this kind of interference.
It also helps to vary the setting in which material is studied.
Memories tied to many cues are easier to find later.
--- page 3 ---
Attention can be directed in two broad ways.
Top-down attention is guided by our goals, as when we search a crowded room for a friend.
Bottom-up attention is captured by the world, as when a loud noise makes us turn our heads.
The two systems often compete.
Advertisers exploit bottom-up capture with bright colours and motion, while good study habits rely on top-down control.
Divided attention has clear costs.
People who try to read while listening to speech remember less of both.
Students who study with their phones nearby check them often, and each check breaks the flow of encoding.
The cost is not only the time lost.
After a switch, it takes several seconds to rebuild the mental context of the task.
These findings suggest simple strategies.
Remove distractions before starting a hard task.
Work in focused blocks with short breaks between them.
Test yourself rather than rereading, because retrieval practice strengthens memory more than passive review.
Finally, sleep well, since sleep helps to consolidate what was learned.
Short walks and a glass of water between study blocks also help many students stay alert.
None of these habits is dramatic on its own, but together they can change how much is remembered a week later.
Small changes, kept up over a whole term, add up to large gains.
